_comment: Platform tool risk table. This is the top policy layer: an AgentVersion
may raise a tool's risk or tighten what a risk level costs, never lower
either. Edit this file (or set TOOL_RISK_POLICY_JSON / point
TOOL_RISK_POLICY_PATH elsewhere) to change which tools need approval.
2026-08-31 (ADR 0009 D4): keys are the DSH factory tool names, not the old
Pi ones. The single source for the names is
agent/src/runtime/policy/tool-names.ts (SANDBOX_TOOL_NAMES); startup asserts
every non-mcp key here exists there and throws otherwise, because the
classifier is fail-closed and a stale key's only symptom would be that its
tool is silently denied at runtime.
Retired in this stage and therefore absent: ls, find, python, process_*,
skill_list/install/create/edit/uninstall, spawn_subagent, check_subagent,
ask_user, todo_read, memory_write, memory_search, submit_artifact.
Old AgentVersion snapshots that still name them are projected through
LEGACY_TOOL_NAME_ALIASES on read; they are not migrated.
riskApproval maps each risk level to what it costs. Approval decisions are
derived from risk only — there is no separate approval switch per tool.
classRiskLevels is the fallback risk for tools with no explicit entry:
local_low            host tools running against the exec RPC seam
external_readonly    MCP tools explicitly marked read-only
external_high        every other MCP tool (external side effects)
internal_interaction ask_user_question
tools keys accept a projected tool name (read, mcp__github__create_pr),
the server::tool form (github::create_pr), or a trailing-* prefix
(mcp__github__*). Longest matching prefix wins; exact keys beat patterns.
Every MCP server MUST have a mcp__<server>__* prefix entry under tools, not
only exact names: the factory dsh-mcp-client normalizes over-long or invalid
tool names and appends a 12-hex-char hash, and such a name matches no exact
key (ADR 0009 D9). buildRunRiskResolver also floors any unmatched mcp__* at
high, so a missing entry degrades to 'needs approval', never to 'allow'.
mcpServers sets a default risk for a whole MCP server plus per-tool
overrides, so a new tool appearing on a server inherits the server's risk
instead of silently defaulting to external_high.
